name: Padded shoulders / structured jackets
lead: Padded shoulders and structured jackets are a clothing approach used to make the shoulders appear broader and the torso more V-shaped. Fashion shoulder pads are fabric-covered padding sewn inside garments to broaden the look of the shoulders and reduce the appearance of slope [1]. In looksmaxxing communities the practice is discussed as a way to add optical shoulder width without training or surgery.

No studies measuring how padded tailoring changes perceived attractiveness were found. The evidence here is historical and anecdotal: fashion history documents repeated cycles of padded-shoulder styles [1], and forum users describe their own experiences [2][3].
infobox: Optical shoulder width, straighter shoulder line
Jacket padding, structured blazers, adhesive or silicone shoulder inserts (as described by users)

paras: Pads inside a jacket extend the shoulder line beyond the wearer's own frame, and structured construction holds the shape. Fashion sources note that pads can also correct narrow or sloping shoulders and help heavy fabrics hold their shape [1]. This is distinct from protective sports shoulder pads, which are designed for contact sports such as American football and ice hockey [4].

Women's shoulder pads became popular in 1931 through designers such as Elsa Schiaparelli and Marcel Rochas, and grew bulkier and more military in appearance during World War II [1]. Sloped, natural shoulders returned in the mid-1940s, and by the 1960s padding had largely disappeared from women's wear; in menswear, Pierre Cardin's 1960 collection promoted a slim, unpadded look [1].

Padded shoulders returned in the late 1970s, with Yves Saint Laurent among the designers credited with the broad-shouldered trend, and became the signature of 1980s power dressing [1]. In menswear, Armani and Cardin added pronounced pads to jackets in the late 1970s, and many 1980s business suits had fuller shoulders; some designers padded to create a V-shape while others reduced padding to show a muscular build [1]. The style faded in the 1990s and has returned in revivals since [1].

On looksmax.org, one user reported wearing adhesive silicone shoulder inserts and being asked whether he played football and about his workout routine; he said they also made his clavicles look straighter [2]. Another thread asked for brand experiences and described padding as an underrated optimization when done well [3]. Some replies disagreed: one user compared inserts to a male push-up bra and said he preferred building lateral deltoids, while another suggested padding would suit only people with sloping shoulders [3]. These are individual reports and opinions.
No studies found. Published research on shoulder pads concerns protective sports equipment, such as heat stress and injury in American football [5][6], not perceived width or attractiveness.

lore.intro: Forum users describe shoulder pads and structured jackets as a cheap way to add shoulder width, with opinion divided on whether inserts are worthwhile [2][3].

claims.claim: Shoulder pads add visible width and a more athletic look
claims.believers: One poster said adhesive silicone pads led people to ask if he played football and about his routine [2]. Another called padding an underrated looksmaxx when done well [3].
claims.experts: No published studies have tested whether padded tailoring changes perceived attractiveness. Fashion history records that padding is used to broaden the look of shoulders [1].

claims.claim: Pads can straighten sloping clavicles visually
claims.believers: A user said inserts straighten the line of his clavicles even though his frame is already broad [2]; another said they would only make sense for sloping shoulders [3].
claims.experts: Fashion sources describe padding as a way to correct narrow or sloping shoulders [1]; no clinical measurement exists.

claims.claim: Padding is a lower-effort substitute that is not worth using if you can build deltoids
claims.believers: A critic in one thread compared inserts to a push-up bra and said he preferred adding lateral delt muscle [3].
claims.experts: No studies compare padding with training for appearance outcomes.

card.summary: Padded shoulders and structured jackets fake shoulder width with tailoring; fashion history backs the look, but no studies test attractiveness effects.
card.note: No appearance studies; sports-pad research is about protection, not looks.

quick.overview:
Pads and structured tailoring extend the shoulder line so the shoulders look broader and the torso more V-shaped. Fashion has used the effect repeatedly since the 1930s.

In forums some users report positive reactions, while others prefer building muscle instead. No controlled studies exist.
quick.mechanism: Padding sewn into a jacket, or inserts worn on the shoulder, add volume beyond the natural frame and hold a firm outline.
quick.risks: No health risks were documented for fashion padding in the sources reviewed. Sports shoulder pads studied in research are a separate product with heat-stress and injury literature.
